Two Numbers

ParityMental MathLogic
Game: I show you two numbers, one even and one odd. Pick one in your head, do the multiplications I ask, and see if I can name your number.
How to play: Multiply the number you pick by the kind of number shown and the other by the other kind. Add the two products, type the sum and press Guess or Enter; press Try again for new numbers.

Choose one of the numbers:

Multiply the number you chose by any odd number.

Multiply the other number by any even number.

Add the two products and type in the sum below.

Look for the math

You pick one of two numbers in secret, yet the computer can name it from a single sum. It is not mind reading: even and odd numbers behave differently when you multiply them.

An even product and a maybe-odd one

An even number is a multiple of 2, so even × k = 2 × (n × k) is always even. An odd number stays odd only when its multiplier is odd; multiply it by an even number and it becomes even too. This is an invariant: multiplying by an even number always destroys parity, while multiplying by an odd number keeps it. So of the two products, one is certainly even and the other is odd exactly when the odd number got the odd multiplier.

Reading the sum

Adding an even number does not change the parity of the other product: even + odd = odd and even + odd×odd = odd. The sum is odd precisely when the odd number received the odd multiplier. The applet's instructions tell you whether that multiplier went to your number or to the other one:

InstructionOdd sumEven sum
Your number × oddyou picked the odd numberyou picked the even number
Your number × evenyou picked the even numberyou picked the odd number

The logic test checked all 5,000 honest plays: five even numbers (2 to 10), five odd numbers (1 to 9), both orders, both instructions, and every small odd or even multiplier. The announced number was the chosen one every time. The page's claim holds; the applet does not name the other number.

What the applet actually reads

Its Guess(sum) compares sum % 2 (Java's remainder) with whether your number was meant to get the odd multiplier. If they match it says the odd number; if not, the even number. That is the table above, written in code. But it never checks how big your sum is: type a sum with the opposite parity and it will confidently name the other number. It reads what you typed, not your working. Java's remainder also keeps a minus sign, so a negative odd sum such as -3 falls down the "even" branch, unlike +3; the logic test checks that quirk too.

Pick a number, work out the real sum, and then type a sum with the other parity. Which number does the computer name? Now try a negative sum and see whether it agrees.
